title: Ion trap on borosilicate substrate with integrated femtosecond-laser-written waveguide
authors: Jakob Wahl, Alexander Zesar, Philipp Hurdax, Marco Schmauser, Victoria Schwab, Michael Pasquini, Marco Valentini, Clemens Rössler, Thomas Monz, Bernhard Lamprecht, Klemens Schüppert, Philipp Schindler
abstract: We present an ion-trap platform on borosilicate glass with an integrated femtosecond-laser-written waveguide for on-chip light delivery. The optical layer is physically separated from the electrode substrate and bonded atop the trap, remaining compatible with silicon-based integration. We engineer single-mode low-loss guidance at 729 nm with tunable mode-field diameter and achieve low-loss curved waveguides down to a radius of curvature of 6 mm. We also extend single-mode operation to a wavelength of 405 nm. The fabrication process is compatible with the industrial fabrication of a single-metal-layer surface-electrode trap, including active fiber alignment and bonding. We validate the platform in a cryogenic trapped-ion system with $^{40}$Ca$^+$, demonstrating trapping, shuttling the ion to a zone in front of the waveguide, and coherent operations driven by 729 nm light delivered through the integrated waveguide. We characterize the effect of the exposed dielectric on the ion and measure stray electric fields that show slow drift at a timescale of hours. The architecture is compatible with hybrid micro-optics (e.g. pick-and-place lenses) to realize single ion addressing and provides a robust, scalable route to integrated light delivery for trapped-ion devices.
summary: This paper presents an advanced ion trap platform built on borosilicate glass featuring an integrated waveguide written by femtosecond lasers. This architecture solves the challenge of routing optical signals in large-scale trapped-ion quantum processors. By demonstrating trapping and coherent operations using this on-chip light delivery, it offers a robust and scalable route for future quantum computing devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is developing a scalable platform for trapped-ion quantum computing that requires robust, on-chip delivery of optical light to address individual qubits.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated an end-to-end system integrating an ion trap on borosilicate glass with an integrated, low-loss waveguide capable of delivering coherent light for qubit operations.
method: They fabricated the platform using femtosecond laser writing (FLW) to create waveguides bonded atop a surface-electrode ion trap and validated functionality in a cryogenic trapped-ion system.
model_or_system: The physical system is an ion trap built on borosilicate glass, featuring aluminum electrodes and an integrated waveguide. The light delivery mechanism physically separates the optical layer from the electrode substrate, enabling compatibility with silicon integration.
key_observables: Coherent Rabi oscillations driven by 729 nm light delivered through the waveguide; measurement of stray electric fields showing slow drift over hours.
important_parameters: Single-mode low-loss guidance at 729 nm and 405 nm; curved waveguides maintained down to a radius of curvature of 6 mm.
main_assumptions: The architecture relies on bonding an optically structured block onto the trap surface, and that positive refractive index changes induced by femtosecond laser exposure are sufficient for guiding weakly guided modes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the concept showing the integrated waveguide positioned in-plane with the ion addressing zone; other figures detail waveguide writing setups and mode profile tuning based on focus offset.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for scalable optical access to presenting the physical platform, detailing the fabrication of low-loss waveguides, and finally validating the entire system through trapping, shuttling, and coherent quantum operations.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major engineering bottleneck in trapped-ion quantum computing—the integration of photonics. For theorists studying open quantum systems or quantum optics, this provides a concrete platform for modeling light-matter interactions on chip at scale.

Patterned segmented DC electrodes allow for shuttling of the ion between the trapping and the addressing zone. On top of the traps’ surface, another borosilicate glass block is bonded that contains a femtosecond laser-written waveguide for light with 729nm wavelength (red beam), inscribed at a distance to the trap surface that is in-plane with the trapping position of the ion.
